claim: The centrosome is composed of two centrioles surrounded by a microtubule-nucleating pericentriolar material (PCM).
source: The centrosome is composed of two centrioles surrounded by a microtubule-nucleating pericentriolar material (PCM).
evidence: This is a well-established structural description of the centrosome found in the introduction.

claim: Several ectopically-expressed animal centriole components such as SAS-6 are recruited to the SPB in fission yeast.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that several ectopically-expressed animal centriole components such as SAS-6 are recruited to the SPB.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A conserved PCM component, Pcp1/pericentrin, interacts with and recruits SAS-6.
source: We revealed that a conserved PCM component, Pcp1/pericentrin, interacts with and recruits SAS-6.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2C and localization studies in Figure 3.

claim: The interaction between Pcp1/pericentrin and SAS-6 is conserved and important for centriole assembly, particularly its elongation.
source: This interaction is conserved and important for centriole assembly, particularly its elongation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments in both Drosophila cells (Figures 5, 6) and fly spermatocytes (Figure 7).

claim: The conserved calmodulin-binding region of Pcp1/pericentrin is critical for SAS-6 interaction.
source: We further explored how yeasts kept this interaction even after centriole loss and showed that the conserved calmodulin-binding region of Pcp1/pericentrin is critical for SAS-6 interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments shown in Figures 4 and 8.

claim: The PCM not only recruits and concentrates microtubule-nucleators, but also the centriole assembly machinery, promoting biogenesis close by.
source: Our work suggests that the PCM not only recruits and concentrates microtubule-nucleators, but also the centriole assembly machinery, promoting biogenesis close by.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Centrioles are normally formed in coordination with the cell cycle, one new centriole forming close to each existing one, within a PCM cloud.
source: Centrioles are normally formed in coordination with the cell cycle, one new centriole forming close to each existing one, within a PCM cloud (Bettencourt-Dias and Glover, 2007; Fu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The first structure of the centriole to be assembled is the cartwheel, a ninefold symmetrical structure, composed of SAS-6, CEP135/Bld10, STIL/Ana2/SAS-5, amongst others.
source: The first structure of the centriole to be assembled is the cartwheel, a ninefold symmetrical structure, composed of SAS-6, CEP135/Bld10, STIL/Ana2/SAS-5, amongst others (Kitagawa et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2013; Nakazawa et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Centriole elongation is dependent on components such as CPAP/SAS-4.
source: This is followed by centriole elongation through the deposition of centriolar microtubules which is dependent on components such as CPAP/SAS-4 (Kohlmaier et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SAS-6 and CEP135/Bld10 can self-assemble in vitro to generate a ninefold symmetrical cartwheel.
source: Remarkably, SAS-6 and CEP135/Bld10 can self-assemble in vitro to generate a ninefold symmetrical cartwheel (Guichard et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Active PLK4 is known to recruit and phosphorylate STIL, which then recruits SAS-6.
source: In vivo, active PLK4 is known to recruit and phosphorylate STIL, which then recruits SAS-6 (Arquint et al., 2012; Arquint et al., 2015; Moyer et al., 2015; Ohta et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: When centrioles are eliminated in human cells by laser ablation, they form de novo within a PCM cloud.
source: In support of this idea, when centrioles are eliminated in human cells by laser ablation, they form de novo within a PCM cloud (Khodjakov et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of pericentrin in S-phase-arrested CHO cells induces the formation of numerous daughter centrioles.
source: Moreover, exaggeration of the PCM cloud by overexpressing a PCM component, pericentrin, in S-phase-arrested CHO cells, induces the formation of numerous daughter centrioles (Loncarek et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PCM components, γ-tubulin and Spd-5, contribute to centriole assembly in C. elegans.
source: Moreover, PCM components, γ-tubulin and Spd-5, a functional analogue of Drosophila CNN and Hs Cdk5rap2, contribute to centriole assembly in C. elegans (Dammermann et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Downregulation of pericentrin (PLP) in Drosophila leads to fragmented and short centrioles.
source: Downregulation of the PCM in Drosophila, has been shown to lead to: i) fragmented and short centrioles, in the case of pericentrin (PLP) (Martinez-Campos et al., 2004; Roque et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Downregulation of CNN in Drosophila leads to disengaged centrioles.
source: ii) disengaged centrioles, in the case of CNN (Lucas and Raff, 2007; Megraw et al., 2001)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Removal of all PCM components in Drosophila leads to centriole disassembly.
source: and iii) centriole disassembly, in the case of the removal of all PCM components (Pimenta-Marques et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Centrioles were lost in several branches of the eukaryotic tree, concomitantly with the loss of the flagellar structure.
source: While centrioles are ancestral in eukaryotes, they were lost in several branches of the eukaryotic tree, concomitantly with the loss of the flagellar structure (Carvalho-Santos et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Yeasts have a spindle pole body (SPB), a layered structure composed of a centriole-less scaffold that recruits γ-tubulin and other PCM components and nucleates microtubules.
source: Instead of a canonical centrosome, yeasts have a spindle pole body (SPB), a layered structure composed of a centriole-less scaffold that similarly recruits γ-tubulin and other PCM components and nucleates microtubules (Cavanaugh and Jaspersen, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The timing and regulation of SPB biogenesis are similar to the one observed in animal centrosomes.
source: The timing and regulation of SPB biogenesis are similar to the one observed in animal centrosomes (Lim et al., 2009; Kilmartin, 2014; Rüthnick and Schiebel, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Early-diverged basal fungi such as chytrids have a centriole-containing centrosome.
source: It is likely that the animal centrosome and yeast SPB evolved from a common ancestral structure that had centrioles (Figure 1A), as early-diverged basal fungi such as chytrids (e.g. Rhizophydium spherotheca) have a centriole-containing centrosome (Powell, 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The proteins required for centriole biogenesis in animals were not identified in the fungal genomes, with exception of chytrids, which have centrioles.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Carvalho-Santos et al., 2010; Hodges et al., 2010), the proteins required for centriole biogenesis in animals were not identified in the fungal genomes, with exception of chytrids, which have centrioles (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Centriole-PCM connectors were not found in both chytrids and yeasts.
source: Centriole-PCM connectors were not found in both chytrids and yeasts.
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pericentrin and Cdk5rap2 were found in all fungal species.
source: In contrast, when investigating the PCM composition, pericentrin and Cdk5rap2 were found in all fungal species, although the budding yeast Spc110 and Spc72 only share short conserved motifs with pericentrin and Cdk5rap2, respectively (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B, with a citation supporting the motif conservation.

claim: Cam1 and Cdc31 are both highly spread across opisthokonts.
source: Regarding the SPB components, we found that Cam1 and Cdc31 are both highly spread across opisthokonts, which may reflect a conserved module or, alternatively an MTOC-independent conserved function of these proteins.
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Proteins such as Ppc89 and Sid4 could only be found in yeasts, but not in chytrids.
source: On the other hand, we could only find proteins such as Ppc89 and Sid4 in yeasts, but not in chytrids, suggesting that some of the yeast-specific structural building blocks of the SPB appeared after branching into yeasts (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SAS-6-GFP, Bld10-GFP and YFP-SAS-4 co-localized with fission yeast Sid4 to the SPB.
source: Despite the one billion years separating yeasts from animals (Douzery et al., 2004; Parfrey et al., 2011), SAS-6-GFP, Bld10-GFP and YFP-SAS-4 co-localized with fission yeast Sid4 to the SPB (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: YFP-SAS-4 signal was also weakly observed along interphase cytoplasmic microtubules, likely reflecting its microtubule-binding capacity.
source: In addition to the localization on the SPB, YFP-SAS-4 signal was also weakly observed along interphase cytoplasmic microtubules, likely reflecting its microtubule-binding capacity (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2, with a citation supporting the interpretation.

claim: GFP-Plk4 and YFP-Ana2 did not localize to the SPB and existed as foci in the cytoplasm.
source: In contrast, GFP-Plk4 and YFP-Ana2 did not localize to the SPB and existed as foci in the cytoplasm (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Cells expressing centriole proteins which localize to the SPB grew as well as control cells.
source: Cells expressing centriole proteins which localize to the SPB grew as well as control cells, which have no centriole protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting their expression does not impair yeast growth.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SAS-6, Bld10 and SAS-4 all interacted with Pcp1 as revealed by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: Surprisingly, we found that SAS-6, Bld10 and SAS-4, all interacted with Pcp1 as revealed by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The intensity of SAS-6-GFP per SPB was significantly increased in control cells when arrested in prometaphase.
source: The intensity of SAS-6-GFP per SPB was significantly increased in control cells when arrested in prometaphase (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Reduced SAS-6-GFP intensity was observed in the pcp1 mutant both at the permissive and restrictive temperatures.
source: We observed reduced SAS-6-GFP intensity in the pcp1 mutant both at the permissive and restrictive temperatures (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Pcp1 is required for SAS-6 recruitment to the SPB.
source: This indicates that Pcp1 is required for SAS-6 recruitment to the SPB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Bld10-GFP intensity was not reduced, but slightly increased in the pcp1 mutant.
source: Unlike SAS-6, Bld10-GFP intensity was not reduced, but slightly increased in the pcp1 mutant (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The intensity of SAS-4 was reduced in the pcp1 mutant.
source: Although the intensity of SAS-4 was reduced in the pcp1 mutant (Figure 3E and F), we found that the total protein of YFP-SAS-4 was also lower in the pcp1 mutant while that of SAS-6-GFP and Bld10-GFP was comparable in control and pcp1 mutant lysates (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 3E, F, and G.

claim: YFP-SAS-4 might be stabilised by Pcp1 in fission yeast cells.
source: We think that YFP-SAS-4 might be stabilised by Pcp1 in fission yeast cells, and therefore we cannot conclude whether Pcp1 is required for YFP-SAS-4 localization on the SPB.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that total YFP-SAS-4 protein levels are reduced in the pcp1 mutant.

claim: Full-length Pcp1 and its C-terminal region containing the conserved PACT domain interacted strongly with SAS-6.
source: Only full-length Pcp1 and its C-terminal region containing the conserved PACT domain interacted strongly with SAS-6 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The PACT domain localizes to the centriole wall in animals and is required for MTOC targeting both in animal and fungi.
source: The PACT domain localizes to the centriole wall in animals and is required for MTOC targeting both in animal and fungi (Gillingham and Munro, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpressed mCherry-tagged Pcp1 recruited SAS-6-GFP, but not GFP (control), to cytoplasmic foci.
source: Overexpressed mCherry-tagged Pcp1 recruited SAS-6-GFP, but not GFP (control), to such foci (Figure 4D and E), indicating that Pcp1 can ectopically recruit SAS-6.
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: SAS-6-GFP center of mass localizes at ~50 nm distance from both Pcp1-tdTomato and Sid4-tdTomato center of mass.
source: Importantly, SAS-6-GFP center of mass localizes at ~50 nm distance from both Pcp1-tdTomato and Sid4-tdTomato center of mass.
evidence: This is a finding from the SIM analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopically expressed SAS-6-GFP localizes to the core of the SPB.
source: Given that the diameter and height of SPB is 180 nm and 90 nm respectively (Ding et al., 1997), our data suggest that ectopically expressed SAS-6-GFP localizes to the core of the SPB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SIM data and a citation providing SPB dimensions.

claim: The C-terminal coiled-coil region of SAS-6 is required for its localization at the SPB.
source: Similar to what happens in animals, the C-terminal coiled-coil region of SAS-6 is required for its localization at the SPB (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C and D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: SAS-6 accumulated at the SPB before entering mitosis.
source: We observed that SAS-6 accumulated at the SPB before entering mitosis, similar to its described regulation in animals, and also similar to the reported recruitment of Pcp1 to the SPB at that cell cycle stage in fission yeast (Keller et al., 2014; Strnad et al., 2007; Wälde and King, 2014).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SAS-6 interacts with the PACT domain of Drosophila pericentrin ortholog, pericentrin-like protein (PLP).
source: Consistent with the results obtained in fission yeast, SAS-6 interacts with the PACT domain (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The interaction between SAS-6 and the PACT domain is direct.
source: To verify whether this interaction is direct, we validated this result in vitro, by performing in vitro binding assays using purified GST, GST-tagged SAS-6 and His-tagged PACT. GST-SAS-6 was specifically bound to His-PACT, indicating a direct interaction between these two proteins (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the in vitro binding assay shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Overexpressing PACT in cells led to increased recruitment of SAS-6 to centrioles.
source: Indeed, overexpressing PACT in cells led to increased recruitment of SAS-6 to centrioles, suggesting PACT recruits SAS-6 (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: PACT overexpression leads to a significant increase in the percentage of cells with more than four centrioles compared to the EGFP control.
source: Reflecting the increased recruitment of SAS-6 to centrioles, we observed a significant increase in the percentage of cells with more than four centrioles compared to the EGFP control (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: STIL depletion does not completely prevent HsSAS-6 recruitment.
source: However, it has been observed that STIL depletion does not completely prevent HsSAS-6 recruitment, and contribution of STIL does not fully account for centrosomal targeting of HsSAS-6 during interphase (Arquint et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Upon depletion of Ana2 or PLP, SAS-6 intensity per pole was significantly reduced compared to control.
source: Upon depletion of Ana2 or PLP, SAS-6 intensity per pole was significantly reduced compared to control (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Double depletion of Ana2 and PLP caused an additive reduction of SAS-6 intensity.
source: Moreover, double depletion of Ana2 and PLP caused an additive reduction of SAS-6 intensity.
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: SAS-6 is recruited by two complementary pathways, which depend on Ana2 and PLP.
source: This result suggests SAS-6 is recruited by two complementary pathways, which depend on Ana2 and PLP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Co-depletion of Ana2 and PLP leads to stronger reduction in the number of centrioles as compared to the single depletions.
source: We observed that co-depletion of Ana2 and PLP leads to stronger reduction in the number of centrioles as compared to the single depletions, indicating both pathways contribute to centriole biogenesis (Figure 6D,E, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6D, E, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of full-length PLP after PLP depletion rescued the centriole number defect.
source: In contrast, when we expressed full-length PLP after PLP depletion, the centriole number defect was rescued, indicating the specific contribution of PLP for centriole formation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of full-length PLP in the presence of endogenous PLP induced centriole amplification similar to PACT overexpression.
source: Moreover, we noticed that expression of full-length PLP in the presence of endogenous PLP induced centriole amplification similar to PACT overexpression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: PLP RNAi did not affect centriole number in sperm cells.
source: The knockdown of PLP by RNAi did not affect centriole number in sperm cells (Figure 7B and C), suggesting that the STIL/Ana2 pathway recruits sufficient SAS-6 to initiate centriole biogenesis.
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: PLP RNAi led to a decrease in centriole length in spermatocytes.
source: However, PLP RNAi led to a decrease in centriole length, as observed with the PLP mutant in somatic cells (Roque et al., 2018), and to male infertility.
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 7, with a citation to previous work.

claim: PLP RNAi affected SAS-6 recruitment to the basal bodies in spermatocytes.
source: Remarkably, PLP RNAi affected SAS-6 recruitment to the BBs (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: PLP is involved in sperm basal body elongation by recruiting SAS-6.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that PLP is involved in sperm BB elongation by recruiting SAS-6, a phenotype that is further accentuated in tissue culture cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The conserved calmodulin-binding domain (CBD) within the PACT domain is sufficient for interaction with SAS-6.
source: Indeed, similar to the PACT domain, CBD interacted with SAS-6-EGFP (Figure 8B). This result indicates that this conserved segment within the PACT domain is sufficient for interaction with SAS-6.
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 8B.

claim: SAS-6-EGFP, CBD and calmodulin formed a complex.
source: Intriguingly, we found that SAS-6-EGFP, CBD and calmodulin formed a complex (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 8B.

claim: SAS-6-EGFP and calmodulin did not interact directly.
source: Since SAS-6-EGFP and calmodulin did not interact directly, we concluded that the complex forms through the CBD segment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The CBD polypeptide was stabilised in the presence of SAS-6-EGFP, and this was more pronounced with the addition of calmodulin.
source: Moreover, we observed that the CBD polypeptide was stabilised in the presence of SAS-6-EGFP, and this was more pronounced with the addition of calmodulin, suggesting that formation of this complex might stabilize pericentrin (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from Figure 8B.

claim: The binding of SAS-6 and calmodulin to the CBD was not competitive.
source: Since the binding of SAS-6 and calmodulin to the CBD was not competitive, it is likely that these two proteins interact with adjacent but distinct amino acids within the CBD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The fact that pericentrin function and stability has always relied on its interaction with calmodulin has constrained the evolution of the pericentrin´s CBD's local structure, therefore retaining its affinity for SAS-6.
source: Our result suggests that the fact that pericentrin function and stability has always relied on its interaction with calmodulin has constrained the evolution of the pericentrin´s CBD's local structure, therefore retaining its affinity for SAS-6.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and evolutionary considerations.

claim: Animals and fungi diverged from their common ancestor about one billion years ago.
source: It is estimated that animals and fungi diverged from their common ancestor about one billion years ago (Douzery et al., 2004; Parfrey et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The localization of new centrioles is likely to be dictated not just by positive regulatory feedbacks amongst centriole components, but also through the regulation of centriole component localization by the PCM.
source: Therefore, the localization of new centrioles is likely to be dictated not just by positive regulatory feedbacks amongst centriole components, but also through the regulation of centriole component localization by the PCM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The STIL/Ana2-dependent SAS-6 recruitment pathway did not account for all SAS-6 present at the centriole.
source: It had been previously observed that the STIL/Ana2-dependent SAS-6 recruitment pathway did not account for all SAS-6 present at the centriole (Arquint et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014), but alternative pathways for SAS-6 recruitment were not known.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In human cells, SAS-6 was previously seen to co-localize with pericentrin at the proximal end of the centriole where it accumulates from S phase.
source: Given that in human cells, SAS-6 was previously seen to co-localize with pericentrin at the proximal end of the centriole where it accumulates from S phase (Keller et al., 2014), we suggest that pericentrin might recruit SAS-6 at that stage.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila tissue cultured cells, pericentrin forms a ring around the mother centriole and SAS-6 occupies the central region of the centriole.
source: However, in Drosophila tissue cultured cells, it has been shown that pericentrin forms a ring around the mother centriole and SAS-6 occupies the central region of the centriole, indicating that the two proteins may not show overlapping localization (Dzhindzhev et al., 2014; Mennella et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The pericentrin-SAS-6 interaction might be transient and highly dynamic.
source: We propose that the pericentrin-SAS-6 interaction might be transient and highly dynamic and therefore co-localization is more difficult to observe.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the localization patterns observed in different systems.

claim: Self-interaction between the head group of SAS-6 is relatively weak (characterized by micro-molar range dissociation constant).
source: Previous biophysical studies have shown that self-interaction between the head group of SAS-6 is relatively weak (characterized by micro-molar range dissociation constant), which suggested the existence of other factors that contribute to the nine-fold symmetry of the centriole (Cottee et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: STIL/Ana2/SAS-5 forms higher-order assemblies and is likely to concentrate SAS-6 molecules and contribute to cartwheel formation in C. elegans and Drosophila.
source: Indeed, further work revealed that STIL/Ana2/SAS-5 forms higher-order assemblies and it is likely to concentrate SAS-6 molecules and contribute to cartwheel formation in C. elegans and Drosophila (Cottee et al., 2015; Rogala et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pericentrin might concentrate SAS-6 around the PCM-bearing mother centriole, and thus contribute to centriole formation, in particular, its elongation, in addition to the STIL/Ana2 pathway.
source: We propose that pericentrin might also concentrate SAS-6 around the PCM-bearing mother centriole, and thus contribute to centriole formation, in particular, its elongation, in addition to the STIL/Ana2 pathway.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: SAS-6 is important for centriole maintenance.
source: Previous studies showed that SAS-6 is important for centriole maintenance (Izquierdo et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression of a symmetry-changing SAS-6 mutant leads to reduced centriole length in human cells.
source: and expression of a symmetry-changing SAS-6 mutant leads to reduced centriole length in human cells (Hilbert et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: SAS-6 is dynamically recruited to the spermatocyte basal bodies to promote elongation.
source: We recently reported that SAS-6 is dynamically recruited to the spermatocyte BBs to promote elongation (Jana et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Pericentrin regulates centriole length and stability by recruiting a dynamic pool of SAS-6 to the centriole/basal body.
source: Here, our data suggest that pericentrin regulates centriole length and stability by recruiting a dynamic pool of SAS-6 to the centriole/BB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Calmodulin binding is important for pericentrin centriole-targeting, and also for its function and protein stability.
source: Calmodulin binding is important for pericentrin centriole-targeting, and also for its function and protein stability (Galletta et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The fission yeast pcp1-14 mutant, which harbors a point mutation in the residue adjacent to CBD2, exhibits reduced protein stability.
source: Moreover, the fission yeast pcp1-14 mutant, which harbors a point mutation in the residue adjacent to CBD2, also exhibits reduced protein stability (Tang et al., 2014), implying a conserved role of calmodulin binding in stabilizing Pcp1/PLP.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Calmodulin binding to the C-terminal region of Spc110 regulates the interaction between Spc110 and Spc29 in budding yeast.
source: Previous studies in budding yeast suggested that calmodulin binding to the C-terminal region of Spc110 regulates the interaction between Spc110 and a critical inner plaque component, Spc29 (Elliott et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Calmodulin binding might modulate the conformation of pericentrin into an 'active form' which is stable and capable of interacting with the centriole and SPB component(s).
source: Perhaps calmodulin binding modulates the conformation of pericentrin into an 'active form' which is stable and capable of interacting with the centriole and SPB component(s), similarly to the regulation of calmodulin-dependent kinases by calmodulin (Crivici and Ikura, 1995).
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous literature about calmodulin-dependent kinases.

claim: A single amino acid deletion of the conserved lysine residue (3154K) mapped in CBD1 of the human pericentrin gene is associated with microcephalic primordial dwarfism type II (MOPDII).
source: Intriguingly, it is reported that a single amino acid deletion of the conserved lysine residue (3154K) mapped in CBD1 of the human pericentrin gene is associated with a genetic syndrome microcephalic primordial dwarfism type II (MOPDII), characterized with severe developmental anomalies (Kantaputra et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mutation in the evolutionary-conserved PISA motif of the SAS-6 gene is associated with autosomal recessive primary microcephaly.
source: To support this possibility, it is also known that mutation in the evolutionary-conserved PISA (present in SAS-6) motif of the SAS-6 gene (Leidel et al., 2005) that affects its function in centriole formation, is associated with autosomal recessive primary microcephaly (Khan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pericentrin orthologs in fungi play essential roles in microtubule organization, mitotic spindle assembly, and cell cycle regulation similarly as in animals.
source: Indeed, pericentrin orthologs in fungi, play essential roles in microtubule organization, mitotic spindle assembly, and cell cycle regulation similarly as in animals, and their function is dependent on calmodulin-binding (Geiser et al., 1993; Kilmartin et al., 1993; Flory et al., 2002; Fong et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The critical role of the calmodulin-pericentrin interaction for proper microtubule nucleation has been retained in evolution, and constrained the evolution of the pericentrin structure even after other interactors, such as SAS-6, were lost upon centriole loss.
source: We suggest that the critical role of the calmodulin-pericentrin interaction for proper microtubule nucleation has been retained in evolution, and constrained the evolution of the pericentrin structure even after other interactors, such as SAS-6, were lost upon centriole loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and evolutionary considerations.

claim: The yeast SPB evolved from an ancestral centriolar centrosome by a step-wise remodeling process.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that the yeast SPB evolved from an ancestral centriolar centrosome by a step-wise remodeling process: an SPB precursor appeared on the centrosome, interacting with the PCM and replacing the role of the centriole as a PCM-recruiting entity (Ito and Bettencourt-Dias, 2018; McLaughlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Many of the yeast genes can be substituted by human orthologs.
source: It has been shown that many of the yeast genes can be substituted by human orthologs (e.g. rescuing the fission yeast cdc2 mutant with the human CDK1 gene), indicating that critical ancestral functions have been conserved across a billion years (Lee and Nurse, 1987; Osborn and Miller, 2007; Kachroo et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Critical functional modules can retain not only the same function, but also interaction capacities even when a binding partner is completely lost.
source: The present study demonstrated that critical functional modules can retain not only the same function, but also interaction capacities even when a binding partner is completely lost.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.
